chunk_findings.detail: `merged()` assumes the "earlier definition" of a self-extending name lives in a strictly lower layer, so it recurses with `merged(name, cands[-2][2], trail)`. When two files in the *same* layer declare the same `name` and the later one has `extends = "<name>"`, `cands[-2][2] == cands[-1][2]`, so `upto` does not decrease and the identical `cands` list is re-derived forever. chunk_findings.detail: The pattern is validated with `for p in re.findall(_PLACE, pattern)`, but `_PLACE = r"\{(\w+)(?::[^{}]*)?\}"` only matches `{word}` or `{word:spec}`; any brace group that is not of that shape is simply not seen, so validation passes. `expand()` then calls `pattern.format(...)`. chunk_findings.detail: `_check_pattern` passes the raw value of `pattern` straight into `Formatter().parse(pattern)` (and later `pattern.format(...)`), but `pattern` is read with `raw.get("pattern", "")` and is not type-checked before this call — the `_typed(src, raw, "pattern", str, ...)` check (if present) only runs later, inside the `DocType(...)` construction that `_check_pattern` precedes. Any non-string TOML value reaches `string.Formatter().parse`, which requires a `str` and raises `TypeError` (e.g. "expected str instance, int found"), and `TypeError` is not in the `except (ValueError, KeyError, IndexError)` tuple, so it escapes as an unhandled traceback instead of the promised file:line error. Concrete input: a TOML doctype with `name = "x"`, `multi = true`, `pattern = 5` (or `pattern = ["docs/{slug}.md"]`). `multi` is `True`, the two `multi`/`path` guards fall through (`pattern` is truthy), and `_check_pattern` crashes before the loader can report anything, violating the stated "every error names the file" contract. Adding `TypeError` to the caught tuple (or validating `pattern` with `_typed` before calling `_check_pattern`) makes this input produce the intended `pattern` error.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_merge` assumes a child's `validate`/`review` value is a mapping and splats it: `out[k] = {**parent.get(k, {}), **child[k]}`. If it is not a mapping, this raises a bare `TypeError`, not the promised `DocTypeError` naming the file. Repro: layer 0 `a.toml` = `[doctype]
name="parent"
path="docs/p.md"`, layer 1 `b.toml` = `[doctype]
name="child"
path="docs/c.md"
extends="parent"
review = true`, then `resolve([...])` evaluates `{**{}, **True}` and blows up with `TypeError: 'bool' object is not a mapping`, even though `_review`/`_validate` were written to reject exactly this with `review must be a table` / `validate must be a table`. The non-extends path reaches those clean checks (`build` → `_review`/`_validate`); the extends path crashes before them, so a plausible user typo (`review = true`, `validate = "..."`) yields a traceback instead of a file:line error in `ddflow doc types validate`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/doctypes/spec.py:278-280 (`_merge`)

chunk_findings.detail: Duplicate section ids inside an extending type are silently collapsed instead of refused. `_merge` stores child sections in a dict keyed by `id` and, on a repeated id, does `secs[s["id"]] = {**secs[s["id"]], **s}`, so the last occurrence overwrites the earlier one; `build`/`_sections` (spec.py:314-316) only detect duplicates in the list it receives, which by then has been deduplicated. So a child such as `extends = "parent"` plus two `[[doctype.section]]` blocks both with `id = "intro"` is accepted with data loss (the second wins), whereas the same descriptor without `extends` raises `duplicate section id 'intro'`. The stated requirement "a type with a duplicate section id is refused" therefore holds only for non-extending types; validation should run before the id-keyed merge, or the merge should reject a repeated id.

`_merge` validates that `child["validate"]` and `child["review"]` are tables, but the very next statement iterates the child's `section` value with `for s in child.get("section", [])` without first checking it is iterable. chunk_findings.detail:
`_sections` uniquifies anchors by counting only the *base* slug: `seen[slug] = seen.get(slug, -1) + 1; anchor = slug if not seen[slug] else f"{slug}-{seen[slug]}"`. It never checks whether the resulting anchor is already in use, so a heading whose slug is literally another slug plus a numeric suffix collides with an already-issued anchor, and both sections then emit chunks with the same `chunk_id`. Concrete input:

```
# Install

a

# Install 1

b

# Install

c
```

The first heading gives `github_anchor("Install") == "install"` with `seen["install"] == 0` → anchor `install`. The second gives slug `install-1`, which is unseen, so → anchor `install-1`. The third again has slug `install`, now `seen["install"] == 1`, so → anchor `install-1` — the *same* anchor as the "Install 1" section. Both sections number their chunks from 0, so `chunk` emits ids such as `path#install-1~0` twice, violating the "stable/unique chunk id = path#anchor~ordinal" contract that the module is built around (citation, dedup, incremental re-index). GitHub's slugger avoids this by incrementing until the candidate anchor is free (yielding `install-2` here); the intent explicitly says anchors are "computed as GitHub does". The fix is to track the set of *emitted* anchors and bump the suffix until an unused one is found.

chunk_findings.detail:
The merge branch of `_pack` (the `if cur and cur[0][2:] == (kind, reg)` case) hands the raw range `[cur[0][0], b)` to `_split_prose`, and that range necessarily contains the blank line(s) that separated the small prose block from the following oversize prose block. `_split_prose` treats those blanks as ordinary lines, so when the first packed chunk ends on a blank line, the overlap loop pulls the blank forward and the next chunk is emitted with `text == ""`. With the defaults, `chunk("x.md", "# H

" + "x"*2000)` returns chunks `"# H
"`, `""`, `"x"*1500`, `"x"*500`: the empty chunk has `line_start == line_end == 2` and the sha256 of the empty string. It reproduces with explicit parameters too, e.g. `chunk("x.md", "aaaa

" + "b"*25, max_chars=20, overlap=5)` yields a chunk with empty text on the blank line. `_blocks` documents that blank lines are dropped, and a chunk with empty content and a line range covering a blank line is wrong; it also perturbs the ordinal numbering of all later chunks in the section.

chunk_findings.detail: `_blocks` computes the region cut positions (`cuts = {r.line_start - 1} | {r.line_end}`) but only enforces them while extending a prose block. For `kind != "prose"` the code does `j = last + 1` with no cut check, so a code fence or table that contains a ddflow region boundary is emitted as one block spanning that boundary, and `_region_of(regions, i)` assigns it only the region of its first line. Given a file whose first line is a fence (```), whose second line is a region marker, and whose remaining lines close the fence, with `RegionSpan(doc, name, line_start=2, line_end=2)`, `_region_of(regions, 0)` returns -1, so the resulting chunk has `region == ""` and `ownership == "human"` even though line 2 is inside the region; the chunk also crosses the region boundary. chunk_findings.detail:
A valid AsciiDoc two-line section title is parsed as a listing-block delimiter. AsciiDoc allows the title to be followed by a line of `-` (also `=`, `~`, `^`, `+`) at least as long as the title, e.g. `Installation\n------------`. Line 109 evaluates `_ADOC_BLOCK` (which matches *any* run of 4+ dashes) before `_ADOC_HEAD`, so the underline is taken as an opening `----` block: `close` becomes the 12-dash string and the loop scans to the next line stripping to exactly that string. Given
```
= Doc

Installation
------------

== Next
```
`heads` contains only `= Doc`; the `Installation` heading is dropped, and because the opener never closes, `sc.code.append((i, n-1))` marks the whole remainder (including `== Next`, whose heading check is skipped by `i = j + 1`) as a code span. So chunk ids/heading_path are wrong and the tail of the document can never be split. The related two-line forms with `~`/`^`/`+` underlines are not recognized as headings at all, so AsciiDoc two-line headings are effectively unsupported while the `-` form is actively harmful.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_scan_rst` never appends to `sc.code` or `sc.table`, although the module docstring states each scanner returns "the line spans of code blocks and tables". RST literal blocks (`text::` + indented block) and `.. code-block::` directives therefore never produce a code span, so the chunker sees this content as prose and will split it at blank lines (and report `kind=prose`). Given
```
Install
=======

Run::

    pytest -q

    coverage report
```
the blank line inside the literal block is a paragraph break, so the block is cut into two chunks even though it is one code sample; for Markdown/AsciiDoc the same input would be protected by `scan.code`. RST tables are likewise never reported (`kind=table` is unreachable for `rst`).

`_split_prose` appends a chunk unconditionally, even when the range it covers contains only blank lines, so the chunker can emit a chunk whose `text` is `""` and whose `sha256` is the digest of the empty string. Reachability: `_pack` re-splits the whole range `[cur[0][0], b)` when an oversize prose block follows other prose blocks in the same region (`if cur and cur[0][2:] == (kind, reg): a = cur[0][0]`, line 263), and that merged range contains the blank lines between the earlier blocks. Concretely, chunk `"# Title

" + "x"*1500 + "
"` (max_chars your default 1500): `_blocks` yields `(0,1,prose,-1)` (the heading line) and `(2,3,prose,-1)` (the 1500-char line); `_pack` merges them and calls `_split_prose(lines, 0, 3, -1, 1500, 150)`; the first chunk ends at `e=2`, the overlap back-off (`while back - 1 > s and size + len(lines[back-1]) + 1 <= overlap`) walks `back` from 2 to 1 because `lines[1]` is the blank line, so `s = 1`; the next pass has `e == s+1` (only the blank fits, since `0 + 1 + 1500 > 1500`), `len(lines[1]) = 0` is not `> max_chars`, so the `else` branch runs `out.append((1, 2, "prose", -1, "
".join(lines[1:2])))` → `(1, 2, "prose", -1, "")`. ==============

The setext-heading branch is gated on two conditions that reject perfectly valid setext headings, so `heads` silently loses them (and with it the heading path, chunk id and split point downstream).

```

```

=====

chunk_findings.detail:
`_split_prose` appends a chunk unconditionally, even when the range it covers contains only blank lines, so the chunker can emit a chunk whose `text` is `""` and whose `sha256` is the digest of the empty string. Reachability: `_pack` re-splits the whole range `[cur[0][0], b)` when an oversize prose block follows other prose blocks in the same region (`if cur and cur[0][2:] == (kind, reg): a = cur[0][0]`, line 263), and that merged range contains the blank lines between the earlier blocks. Concretely, chunk `"# Title

" + "x"*1500 + "
"` (max_chars your default 1500): `_blocks` yields `(0,1,prose,-1)` (the heading line) and `(2,3,prose,-1)` (the 1500-char line); `_pack` merges them and calls `_split_prose(lines, 0, 3, -1, 1500, 150)`; the first chunk ends at `e=2`, the overlap back-off (`while back - 1 > s and size + len(lines[back-1]) + 1 <= overlap`) walks `back` from 2 to 1 because `lines[1]` is the blank line, so `s = 1`; the next pass has `e == s+1` (only the blank fits, since `0 + 1 + 1500 > 1500`), `len(lines[1]) = 0` is not `> max_chars`, so the `else` branch runs `out.append((1, 2, "prose", -1, "
".join(lines[1:2])))` → `(1, 2, "prose", -1, "")`. The resulting `Chunk` has `text=""`, `line_start==line_end==2` (a blank line), and a hash equal to every other empty chunk's hash. `_split_prose` should skip blank lines when advancing `s` (or drop chunks whose text is empty after stripping), otherwise any document with a short block followed by a blank line and a ≥1500-character line gains a spurious content-free chunk.

chunk_findings.detail:
The setext guard `(i == start or not lines[i - 1].strip())` requires the line above the underline to itself start a paragraph, so multi-line setext headings — legal CommonMark and rendered as headings by GitHub — are never detected, and the affected content is attributed to the enclosing section instead of getting its own heading, heading path and anchor. For `"Title line one
Title line two
==============
"`, `i=0` fails because `lines[1]` is not an underline, and `i=1` fails the guard because `lines[0]` is non-blank, so `sc.heads` stays empty and `_sections` returns a single anchorless section (`first=start, stop=len(lines)`), whereas GitHub produces an `<h1>` with anchor `title-line-one-title-line-two`. The heading text of a setext heading is the whole preceding paragraph, not just its last line; the guard should look for the start of the paragraph run rather than requiring an immediately preceding blank line.

chunk_findings.detail:
The setext-heading branch is gated on two conditions that reject perfectly valid setext headings, so `heads` silently loses them (and with it the heading path, chunk id and split point downstream).

(a) Line 61, `not ln.lstrip().startswith(("|", ">", "-", "*", "+"))`, treats *any* line whose first non-space character is `-`, `*` or `+` as a list/quote/table and refuses to make it a heading — but a list marker requires a following space. Input:

```
**Note**
========
```
`**Note**` is a plain paragraph (the `*` is followed by `*`, not a space, so it is not a list item) and `========` is a setext underline, so CommonMark yields an H1 "Note"; the scanner returns `heads == []` because `"**Note**".lstrip().startswith("*")` is true. The same happens for `*emphasis*`, `+Add flag`, `-Werror`, etc. A correct guard would require `-`/`*`/`+` followed by whitespace.

(b) Line 59, `(i == start or not lines[i - 1].strip())`, additionally requires a blank line before the heading text, but a block boundary (a closing code fence, an ATX heading, a table) is also a paragraph start. Input:

```
Intro

```
make
```
Build
=====
```
At the line `Build`, `lines[i-1]` is the closing ```` ``` ````, which is non-blank, so the setext branch is skipped and "Build" is never reported as a heading, even though CommonMark makes it a setext H1 (the fence ends the previous block). The same input shape after an ATX heading or a table under-reports headings.

chunk_findings.detail:
The table test only requires two consecutive lines starting with `|`; it never checks for the GFM header-delimiter row that actually makes a table. Input:

```
The pipeline prints:
| sort
| uniq -c
```
`lines[1].lstrip().startswith("|")` and `lines[2].lstrip().startswith("|")` are both true, so the scanner appends `table = [(1, 2)]` and the chunker will treat two ordinary paragraph lines as a table (kind `table`, no split). Rendered Markdown/GFM treats these as prose, not a table, because no delimiter row (`| --- |`) follows the header.

chunk_findings.detail:
The table test accepts any delimiter row matched by `_DELIM`, without checking the two conditions GFM actually imposes: the delimiter row must contain a pipe, and it must have the same number of cells as the header row ("The header row must match the delimiter row in the number of cells. If they do not match, a table will not be recognized"). The last conjunct, `"|" in lines[i + 1] + ln`, cannot enforce either: the first conjunct already requires a pipe in `ln`, so the concatenation always contains one — the clause is dead. Demonstrated inputs: (a) `"Use grep | sort
---
"` — `_DELIM` matches `---` (its `\|?`/`:(…)?` parts are all optional), so lines 0–1 become a `table` span; GFM has no table here (delimiter row has no pipes / 1 cell vs 2) and instead renders line 0 as a setext `h2`, so the heading, its heading path and its anchor are lost and the chunk is never split. (b) `"| a | b |
| --- |
| x |
"` — 2-cell header vs 1-cell delimiter row; GFM treats all three lines as one paragraph (the spec's own mismatch example), while this code emits a table. Fixing it means either requiring a pipe in `lines[i+1]` or comparing cell counts.

chunk_findings.detail:
The title is taken as exactly the single line `a` immediately above the adornment (`text = a.strip()`), but reStructuredText section titles may span several lines (the title text is the whole block preceding the underline). Input:

```
Install the tool
from source
===========
```

docutils makes one section titled `Install the tool\nfrom source`; this scanner starts the loop at `i=0`, finds `lines[1]` is not an adornment, advances, and then matches at `i=1`, emitting a heading `("from source", line 1)`. The first line of the real title is attributed to the enclosing section, the chunk boundary moves, and the heading path/anchor become `from-source` instead of the slug of the full title — the same class of defect that was confirmed for multi-line Markdown setext headings, but in the new RST code. The same one-line assumption also makes the length check (`len(under.rstrip()) >= len(text)`, line 116) compare the underline against the last line only rather than the longest title line.

chunk_findings.detail: The setext branch is gated on `not _LIST.match(ln)`, and `_LIST`'s second alternative is the blanket `^\s*[>|]`, which treats *any* paragraph starting with `|` as a list/quote/table. For `"| foo\n===\n"` the table branch does not fire (`===` is not a delimiter row), so the setext branch is the only chance, and it is suppressed: the scanner emits two prose lines, whereas GFM renders an `h1` with the text `| foo`. (The `>` half of that alternative is justified — a line starting with `>` is a blockquote — but the `|` half rejects a legal paragraph, the same mistake the previous finding 3 identified for `-`/`*`/`+`.)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_rst_title` builds the title as `rows = [r.strip() for r in lines[first:k]]`, i.e. it strips each candidate line and accepts *any* run of non-blank lines up to the first adornment, with no requirement that those lines share an indentation level. An indented block that ends immediately before a section title (no blank line) is therefore absorbed into the title, and because the failed/odd candidate is consumed with one `i += 1` while `fresh` is cleared, the real title is never examined. Input:

```
Example::

    x = 1
Usage
=====
```
Trace: i=0 (`Example::`) returns None at the blank line at i=1, so `fresh=False`; i=2 is `    x = 1` with `fresh=True` (previous line blank), `over=False`, `first=2`, loop hits `lines[4] = "====="`, `rows = ["x = 1", "Usage"]`, `long_enough` is `5 >= max(5,5)` → true, so the scanner appends the heading `("x = 1 Usage", '=', False)` at line 2 and sets `i = 5`. The document therefore gets a bogus section whose anchor is `x-1-usage`, starting at the literal block's line, and the genuine `Usage` heading is never emitted (its content is attributed to the enclosing section). In RST an indentation change ends the preceding block, so the title here is exactly `Usage`; only lines of the same indentation can form one title. (The same merge happens for any indented block, e.g. directive content or a `::` literal block, whose last line is short enough for the following underline to satisfy `long_enough`.)

chunk_findings.detail:
Because `_scan_rst` only calls `_rst_title` when `fresh` is true, and any non-blank line that fails to start a title sets `fresh = False`, a heading can no longer start at a line that follows another same-block line — even when that other line is a complete block by itself. Input:

```
.. _install:
Install
=======
```
i=0 (`.. _install:`) runs `_rst_title`, which scans to the adornment at i=2 and returns None (`max(len)` of `".. _install:"`/`"Install"` is 13 > 7), so `fresh` becomes False; i=1 (`Install`) and i=2 (`=======`) are then processed by the `else` branch only, so no heading is emitted at all. The pre-rewrite scanner examined every line (`elif a.strip() and ... _RST_ADORN.match(lines[i + 1])`), and docutils also treats the explicit target as its own block (it emits the informational "ends without a blank line" message and still makes `Install` a section), so this is a dropped heading: the section loses its heading path, anchor and chunk id and its body is merged into the parent. Same for a `.. comment` line immediately preceding a title.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_cells` counts cells with `len(row.strip().strip("|").split("|"))`: `str.strip("|")` removes *all* leading/trailing pipes and the split is not escape-aware, so the count diverges from GFM. GFM requires pipes inside a cell to be escaped (`\|`), and an escaped pipe does not separate cells; input

```
| `cat \| wc -l` | lines |
| --- | --- |
| `a` | 1 |
```
is a two-column table on GitHub, but `_cells("| \`cat \\| wc -l\` | lines |")` returns 3 while the delimiter row returns 2, so `_is_table_head` rejects it, the two rows are emitted as `kind=prose`, and the table rows become prose text/boundaries (the old `"|" in …` test did accept it). Symmetrically, `.strip("|")` collapses repeated border pipes (`|| a` counts 1 instead of 2), so a genuine two-cell header can be mis-compared against its delimiter row in either direction.
